AgentCore Gateway converts existing APIs (from OpenAPI specs) and Lambda functions into MCP tools, with inbound and outbound authentication, without rewriting them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API Gateway with shared keys: doesn't speak MCP, and shared keys are weak.
• Knowledge base of specs: agents could read specs but not call APIs.
• Step Functions wrappers: not MCP tool discovery.

Key takeaway: expose existing APIs as MCP tools → AgentCore Gateway.
Q001977:
Why this is correct:
The refund tool starts a Step Functions workflow that pauses on a task token until a supervisor approves or rejects, which can take hours or days, enforcing policy outside the model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Denied topic: blocks discussion, not an approval step.
• Lower temperature: probabilistic, not a control.
• Prompt instruction: the model can skip it.

Key takeaway: mandatory approvals belong in deterministic workflows.
Q001978:
Why this is correct:
ConverseStream returns tokens as they're generated, and Lambda response streaming (or a WebSocket API) relays them to the browser so users see text immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch and poll: slower and asynchronous.
• Lower maxTokens: truncates answers.
• More Lambda memory: doesn't speed model generation.

Key takeaway: long answers → stream them.
Q001979:
Why this is correct:
Batch inference processes JSONL input from S3 asynchronously at a discount versus on-demand, which suits 500,000 overnight summaries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Throughput: commitment-based and not cheaper for a nightly burst.
• ConverseStream: interactive streaming.
• Lambda fleet on-demand: full price and throttling risk.

Key takeaway: overnight bulk + cost focus → batch inference.
Q001980:
Why this is correct:
A supervisor agent breaks down the request, delegates to the flight, hotel, and visa collaborators, and combines their results through one entry point.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Three knowledge bases without actions: can't perform bookings or checks.
• Call all three and concatenate: wasteful and incoherent.
• One merged action group: tool selection degrades as tools grow.

Key takeaway: multiple specialist domains → supervisor with collaborators.
Q001981:
Why this is correct:
The contextual grounding check scores grounding (support in the source) and relevance (addresses the query), and blocks responses below the thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Denied topics: subject restrictions.
• Word filters: exact terms only.
• Sensitive information filters: PII patterns.

Key takeaway: unsupported or off-topic answers → contextual grounding check.
Q001982:
Why this is correct:
Automated Reasoning checks convert the written policy into formal logic and verify whether answers are logically consistent with it, with explanations of the findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grounding check: statistical comparison with text, not logical verification.
• Prompt attack filters: jailbreak detection.
• A second model's opinion: not a verification.

Key takeaway: logical policy compliance → Automated Reasoning checks.
Q001983:
Why this is correct:
An interface endpoint for bedrock-runtime gives private access without internet, and its endpoint policy can allow InvokeModel only on the two approved model ARNs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway endpoint: exists only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• S3 gateway endpoint: doesn't reach Bedrock.
• NAT gateway: uses the internet path and can't restrict models.

Key takeaway: private access + model restrictions → interface endpoint with a policy.
Q001984:
Why this is correct:
The bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition key lets policies deny invocations that don't include the approved guardrail, which prevents calls without it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store reference: relies on developers.
• Logging and alerting: detective, not preventive.
• Attach to the model: guardrails are applied per request, not attached to models.

Key takeaway: enforce guardrail use with IAM conditions.
Q001985:
Why this is correct:
Invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs captures prompts and responses, and a log group data protection policy masks email addresses and card numbers, with unmasking limited to principals with logs:Unmask.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable logging and use CloudTrail: no payloads.
• S3 with encryption: stores the raw sensitive data.
• Token counts only: fails the audit requirement.

Key takeaway: full logs without exposing PII → masking data protection policies.
Q001986:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent prompt routing sends simpler requests to a smaller model and complex ones to a larger model in the same family, without custom routing code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch inference: asynchronous.
• Cross-Region inference: capacity, not cheaper models.
• Provisioned Throughput: a commitment, not per-request model choice.

Key takeaway: mixed difficulty without custom code → intelligent prompt routing.
Q001987:
Why this is correct:
An application inference profile per application gives each its own invocation identity, so token metrics and tagged costs can be split per application.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency as a cost proxy: inaccurate.
• Character-based estimates: inaccurate.
• Account per application: heavy and only monthly.

Key takeaway: per-app cost attribution → application inference profiles.
Q001988:
Why this is correct:
A semantic cache matches questions by meaning (embedding similarity), so paraphrased questions reuse stored answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher temperature: unrelated.
• Prompt caching: reuses processing of identical prefixes, not answers to paraphrases.
• Exact-match cache: misses paraphrases.

Key takeaway: paraphrased repeats → semantic cache.
Q001989:
Why this is correct:
Latency-optimized inference is offered for selected models and Regions to reduce latency at a different price, which fits a voice use case willing to pay more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch: asynchronous.
• Global cross-Region: throughput and resilience, not lower latency.
• Higher maxTokens: doesn't reduce TTFT.

Key takeaway: lowest latency, higher price → latency-optimized inference.
Q001990:
Why this is correct:
A knowledge base evaluation job with an LLM judge scores retrieval (for example, context relevance) and generation (for example, faithfulness) across all 500 questions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BLEU vs. sources: measures overlap, not faithfulness.
• Latency metrics: not quality.
• 10 human-reviewed answers: too small a sample.

Key takeaway: evaluate RAG retrieval and generation at scale.
Q001991:
Why this is correct:
Agents choose tools based on descriptions. Clear, distinct action and parameter descriptions (what each returns and when to use it) fix wrong selections, and traces confirm the reasoning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking 'package': breaks legitimate requests.
• Session timeout: unrelated.
• Embedding model: agents don't choose tools by embeddings here.

Key takeaway: tool confusion → improve descriptions.
Q001992:
Why this is correct:
An evaluation stage in the delivery pipeline scores each prompt change against a golden dataset and blocks promotion when scores drop.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-rating in production: not a gate.
• Higher temperature in staging: adds noise.
• Deploy then roll back on complaints: too late.

Key takeaway: gate prompt changes with automated evaluation.
Q001993:
Why this is correct:
stopReason 'max_tokens' means the output hit the configured limit. Raising maxTokens (within the model's output cap) or generating in sections fixes the truncation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop sequence: ends output earlier, not later.
• Shorter input: input is not the constraint.
• Lower temperature: doesn't guarantee shorter output.

Key takeaway: read stopReason to diagnose truncation.
